chapter.title: Attributes and Styling
chapter.description: Why it is className not class, and how the style prop differs from a CSS string.

blocks.text: JSX attributes look like HTML attributes but they are really props on a JavaScript object. A few names differ because they clash with reserved words or use JavaScript naming conventions.

items: `class` becomes `className`, because `class` is a reserved word.
Most other attributes keep their HTML name: `id`, `src`, `alt`, `href`, `disabled`.

blocks.code:
<label htmlFor="email" className="field-label">
  Email
</label>
<input id="email" type="email" onChange={handleChange} disabled={isBusy} />

blocks.text: Values in braces
Quotes give an attribute a literal string. Braces give it the result of an expression, which can be any type.

blocks.code: {/* the string "/logo.png" */} {/* whatever logoUrl holds */} {/* a boolean */} {/* an array */}

blocks.text: The style prop
Inline styles take an object, not a string, and the property names are camelCased. The double braces you often see are simply an object literal inside a JSX expression.

blocks.caption: Outer braces: a JSX expression. Inner braces: the object itself.

blocks.text: A plain number is treated as pixels for most properties, so `fontSize: 16` means 16px. Properties that are not lengths, such as `lineHeight` or `zIndex`, keep the raw number.
Inline styles cannot express media queries, pseudo-classes or keyframes. Reach for CSS files, CSS modules or a styling library for anything beyond a handful of dynamic values.

previous.title: Embedding Values in JSX
previous.description: Curly braces, which values render, and which quietly disappear.

blocks.text: Curly braces open an escape hatch back into JavaScript. Anything between them is evaluated as an expression and its result is rendered.

blocks.output: Ada published her notes in 1843. That was 183 years ago.

blocks.text: Expressions only, not statements

The braces hold an **expression** - something that produces a value. An `if` statement or a `for` loop is not an expression, so it cannot go inside braces. Use a ternary, `&&`, or `map` instead, or compute the value above the return.
What React renders and what it skips

items: Strings and numbers render as text.
Arrays render each item in order.
Plain objects throw an error - React cannot guess how to display them.

blocks.text:
`{count &&

Items

}` renders a literal `0` when count is zero, because `0` is falsy but is still a renderable number. Write `{count > 0 &&

Items

}` instead.

blocks.code:
{null}          // renders nothing
{false}         // renders nothing
{0}             // renders the character 0
{["a", "b"]}    // renders ab
{{ a: 1 }}      // Error: Objects are not valid as a React child

next.title: Fragments and Structure
next.description: Returning several elements, self-closing tags and the rules JSX enforces.

blocks.text: JSX has a few structural rules that trip people up early. They all come from the same place: JSX compiles to a function call, and a function call returns one value.
One root element
A component returns a single element. Two sibling elements at the top level are a syntax error.
You could wrap them in a `<div>`, but that adds a node to the DOM that may break table or flex layouts. A **fragment** groups children without producing any element.

blocks.caption: `<>...</>` is shorthand for `<Fragment>...</Fragment>`.

blocks.text: The short syntax cannot take props. When you need a `key` - almost always inside a `map` - use `<Fragment key={...}>`.
Every tag must close
HTML lets you leave some tags open. JSX does not: every element is either closed or self-closed.
Comments and whitespace
Comments inside JSX go in braces. Whitespace between lines is collapsed, so use `{" "}` when you need a space React would otherwise drop.

blocks.title: Build a small profile card
blocks.instructions: Return a fragment containing an h3 with the name and a p with the role. Do not add a wrapper div.

tests.name: An h3 shows the name
tests.code: var el = document.querySelector('#root h3'); return !!el && el.textContent.trim() === 'Grace Hopper';

tests.name: A p shows the role
tests.code: var el = document.querySelector('#root p'); return !!el && el.textContent.trim() === 'Computer Scientist';
